first.rationale: Triage logic: the two directions most likely to win the single slot are promotional_pricing (direct answer to the competitor) and onboarding/activation work (direct answer to the two declining metrics). memory_73 is the highest-stakes and weakest-supported belief for this objective — it is credited with 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' but says nothing about margin, retention, or the quality of the accounts acquired, which is exactly what 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' turns on; discount-led acquisition against a competitor's entry price is the classic way to buy revenue that does not persist. memory_86 is the belief my current intent rests on, and it is measured only on proxies (completion rate, time-to-value, early adoption) rather than on revenue that survives; shortening onboarding can also lower the bar in ways that admit weaker accounts. Both are consequential and both are under-evidenced for the objective, so they get the budget. I do not spend a pull on memory_57, which already reports an explicit retention check, nor on memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist does not address the SMB pressure or the two declining metrics this week), nor on memory_31/memory_91, which are lower-stakes variants of the same onboarding/activation thesis I am already testing. Current intent is simplify_onboarding because it is the only direction that plausibly moves both declining metrics at once and does not risk repricing the book, but I am holding it at small_guarded_test scale rather than broad rollout: the supporting evidence is proxy-metric only, the archived records may show short measurement windows or non-comparable segments, and I want downstream qualified-revenue instrumentation (not just completion rate) before scaling. If memory_86's record turns out to be thin or short-horizon, I would shift to activation_messaging; if memory_73's record shows durable margin-adjusted revenue rather than a headline acquisition spike, promotional_pricing becomes defensible as the competitive response.

final.rationale: Verification resolved both pulls decisively and in the direction that matters for the objective. memory_73 turns out to be a distorted summary: the source record (exp_73) shows signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% but 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit conclusion that the discounted cohort does not survive the first renewal cycle and that targeted discounting must NOT be generalized as a sustainable-growth strategy. The inherited memory had preserved the headline lift and dropped the disqualifying caveat. Since the primary objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is ruled out even though it is the most direct-seeming answer to the competitor's entry pricing — matching a discount war would buy a cohort that churns before renewal and would also reprice the existing SMB book. memory_86 verified cleanly: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and critically 30-day retention +3%, so the onboarding gain is not a bar-lowering artifact that admits weaker accounts; it improves a real durable metric. That was my main worry about this direction and it is now retired, which is why I move from small_guarded_test to standard_experiment rather than staying maximally hedged. simplify_onboarding is also the only candidate that addresses both declining metrics at once: onboarding completion is down 4% directly, and activation is down 6% with memory_31 and memory_91 both indicating the signup/onboarding path feeds first-week activation. I decline enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44 is unverified and addresses neither declining metric nor the SMB pressure) and referral_incentive (memory_57 is unverified and referrals amplify an acquisition funnel whose activation is currently degrading). Residual uncertainty I am not collapsing: exp_86 measures retention at 30 days, which is short of the renewal cycle that exposed exp_73's problem, so the durability evidence is real but not yet renewal-horizon; memory_31 and memory_91 remain unverified and may carry the same summary-drift that memory_73 did; and onboarding improvements do not answer the competitor's price pressure, so the SMB pricing threat stays open and should be addressed with a margin-and-retention-instrumented design rather than a discount. I will measure this experiment on qualified revenue that persists past renewal, not on completion rate alone, and I am flagging for the next session that memory_73 should be rewritten to carry its own caveat.
